10:A '''National Landscape''' ({{Langx|cy|Tirwedd Cenedlaethol}}), formally and formerly an '''Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty''' ('''AONB'''; {{Langx|cy|Ardal o Harddwch Naturiol Eithriadol}}, '''AHNE'''), is one of 38 areas of [[rural area|countryside]] in [[England]] and [[Wales]] that has been designated for [[protected area|conservation]] due to its significant landscape value. The current name was adopted in 2023.
12:Areas are designated in recognition of their national importance by the relevant public body: [[Natural England]] or [[Natural Resources Wales]], respectively. On 22 November 2023, following a review, the AONBs in England and Wales adopted the National Landscapes name, and are in the process of rebranding. The name "area of outstanding natural beauty" is still the designated legal term.
16:National Landscapes enjoy levels of protection from development similar to those of [[national parks of the United Kingdom|UK national parks]], but unlike national parks the responsible bodies do not have their own [[Town and country planning in the United Kingdom|planning powers]]. They also differ from national parks in their more limited opportunities for extensive outdoor recreation.<ref name="Gov">{{cite news|url=http://www.naturalengland.org.uk/ourwork/conservation/designations/aonb/|title=Areas of outstanding natural beauty (AONBs): designation and management – GOV.UK|newspaper=Gov.uk|access-date=16 February 2018}}</ref>
18:There are 38 National Landscapes, 33 wholly in England, [[National Landscapes in Wales|four wholly in Wales]] and [[Wye Valley National Landscape|one on the England–Wales border]], as well as a further eight AONBs in [[Northern Ireland]].
21:The idea for what would eventually become the AONB designation was first put forward by [[John Gordon Dower|John Dower]] in his 1945 ''Report to the Government on National Parks in England and Wales''. Dower suggested there was need for protection of certain naturally beautiful landscapes that were unsuitable as national parks owing to their small size and lack of wildness. Dower's recommendation for the designation of these "other amenity areas" was eventually embodied in the [[National Parks and Access to the Countryside Act 1949]] as the AONB designation.<ref name="AONB story">{{cite web|url=http://www.landscapesforlife.org.uk/aonb-story.html|title=NAAONB|access-date=16 February 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170829080922/http://www.landscapesforlife.org.uk/aonb-story.html|archive-date=29 August 2017|url-status=dead}}</ref>
24:The purpose of an AONB designation in England and Wales is to [[landscape-scale conservation|conserve]] and enhance the natural beauty of the designated landscape.<ref name='Gov'/>
26:There are two secondary aims: meeting the need for quiet enjoyment of the countryside and having regard for the interests of those who live and work there. To achieve these aims, AONBs rely on [[town and country planning in the United Kingdom|planning controls]] and practical countryside management. As they have the same landscape quality, AONBs may be compared to the [[national parks of England and Wales]]. National parks are well known in the UK; by contrast, there is evidence to indicate many residents in AONBs may be unaware of the status. However, the National Association of AONBs launched initiatives to increase awareness of AONBs in local communities,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.aonb.org.uk/__80256cd200319c8e.nsf/PublishedContent/e2a6b120d1308d7480256ced0061d328!OpenDocument&AutoFramed|title=NAAONB|access-date=16 February 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140913214618/http://www.aonb.org.uk/__80256cd200319c8e.nsf/PublishedContent/e2a6b120d1308d7480256ced0061d328%21OpenDocument%26AutoFramed|archive-date=13 September 2014|url-status=dead}}</ref> and, in 2014, successfully negotiated to have the boundaries of AONBs in England shown on [[Google Maps]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.suffolkcoastandheaths.org/assets/Publications/Newspaper--Newsletters/Monthly-Updates/SCH-AONB-February-Monthly-Update.pdf|title=Suffolk Coast & Heaths AONB|access-date=16 February 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180928224039/http://www.suffolkcoastandheaths.org/assets/Publications/Newspaper--Newsletters/Monthly-Updates/SCH-AONB-February-Monthly-Update.pdf|archive-date=28 September 2018|url-status=dead}}</ref>
29:[[Image:ThreeCliffsBay.jos.500pix.jpg|thumb|View over [[Three Cliffs Bay]] in the [[Gower Peninsula]], the first designated Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty]]
30:There are 48 "Areas of Outstanding Natural Beauty" in the United Kingdom in total, 33 in England, [[Areas of Outstanding Natural Beauty in Wales|four in Wales]], [[Wye Valley AONB|one on the England–Wales border]], and a further eight AONBs in [[Northern Ireland]]. Those in England and Wales are branded as "National Landscapes". 
32:The first AONB was established in 1956 on the [[Gower Peninsula]] in [[South Wales]], and the most recent to be designated is the [[Tamar Valley AONB]], established in 1995.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.tamarvalley.org.uk/about/what-is-the-tamar-valley-aonb/|title=Tamar Valley - What is the Tamar Valley AONB?|website=www.tamarvalley.org.uk|access-date=16 February 2018}}</ref> More recent changes include the Clwydian Range AONB being extended in 2012 to form the [[Clwydian Range and Dee Valley]] AONB, and in Northern Ireland, the [[Strangford Lough]] and [[Lecale Coast AONB|Lecale Coast]] AONBs were merged to form a single AONB in 2010.<ref name="strangfordandlecale">{{cite web|url=http://www.doeni.gov.uk/niea/de/protected_areas_home/aonb/strangford_and_lecale_aonb-2.htm|title=Northern Ireland Environment Agency|access-date=16 February 2018}}</ref>
34:AONBs vary greatly in terms of size, type and use of land, and whether they are partly or wholly open to the public. The smallest AONB is the [[Isles of Scilly]], {{convert|16|km2|sqmi|abbr=on}}, and the largest is the [[Cotswolds]],<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.cotswoldsaonb.org.uk/about-the-cotswolds/|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20140914181536/http://www.cotswoldsaonb.org.uk/about-the-cotswolds/|url-status=dead|title=Cotswolds AONB|archivedate=14 September 2014}}</ref> {{convert|2038|km2|sqmi|abbr=on}}. AONBs cover around 15% of England and 4% of Wales.<ref>{{Cite web |title=About Areas of Outstanding Natural Beauty (AONB's) |url=https://landscapesforlife.org.uk/about-aonbs/about-aonbs |access-date=2022-04-10 |website=landscapesforlife.org.uk}}</ref>
37:Areas of Outstanding Natural Beauty in [[England and Wales]] (now also National Landscapes) were originally created under the same legislation as the [[national park]]s, the [[National Parks and Access to the Countryside Act 1949]]. Unlike AONBs, national parks have special legal powers to prevent unsympathetic development. AONBs in general remain the responsibility of their local authorities by means of special committees that include members appointed by a [[Secretary of State (United Kingdom)|minister]] and by parishes, and only very limited statutory duties were imposed on local authorities within an AONB by the original 1949 Act. However, further regulation and protection of AONBs in England and Wales was added by the [[Countryside and Rights of Way Act 2000|Countryside and Rights of Way (CRoW) Act 2000]], under which new designations are now made,<ref>[http://www.staffsmoorlands.gov.uk/sites/default/files/documents/pages/CV%20AONB%20Assessment%20Paper.pdf Staffordshire Moorlands District Council] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140911183009/http://www.staffsmoorlands.gov.uk/sites/default/files/documents/pages/CV%20AONB%20Assessment%20Paper.pdf |date=11 September 2014 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.highweald.org/downloads/publications/1093-development-control-information-leaflet/file.html|title=High Weald AONB|access-date=16 February 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180928071108/http://www.highweald.org/downloads/publications/1093-development-control-information-leaflet/file.html|archive-date=28 September 2018|url-status=dead}}</ref>
39:In the [[National Planning Policy Framework]] (March 2012), the government stated that AONBs and national parks have equal status when it comes to planning decisions on landscape issues.  Two of the AONBs (the Cotswolds and the Chilterns), which extend into a large number of local authority areas, have their own statutory bodies, known as conservation boards. In 2019, the [[Julian Glover (journalist)|Glover Report]] made various recommendations regarding the future of AONBs{{snd}}the report's 'central proposal' being to bring [[National parks of the United Kingdom|National Parks]] and AONBs together as part of one 'family of national landscapes'.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Landscapes review: National Parks and AONBs |url=https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/designated-landscapes-national-parks-and-aonbs-2018-review |access-date=2022-06-03 |website=GOV.UK |date=25 September 2019 |language=en}}</ref> Following the report the Cotswolds Conservation Board announced in September 2020 that they were re-styling the area name and it is now known as the Cotswolds National Landscape.<ref>{{cite web |title=Latest News: The Cotswolds AONB gets a new look and a new name |url=https://www.cotswoldsaonb.org.uk/about-us/latest-news/ |website=Cotswolds National Landscape |publisher=Cotswolds AONB |access-date=31 October 2020}}</ref> The UK Government later accepted the report's recommendation for the AONBs in England to use "National Landscape".<ref>{{Cite web |title=Landscapes review (National Parks and AONBs): government response |url=https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/landscapes-review-national-parks-and-aonbs-government-response/landscapes-review-national-parks-and-aonbs-government-response |access-date=2026-02-23 |website=GOV.UK |language=en}}</ref>
41:All English and Welsh AONBs have a dedicated AONB officer and other staff. As required by the CRoW Act, each AONB has a management plan that sets out the characteristics and special qualities of the landscape and how they will be conserved and enhanced. The AONBs are collectively represented by the "National Landscapes Association",<ref>{{Cite web |title=National Landscapes - Our Story |url=https://national-landscapes.org.uk/about |access-date=2026-02-23 |website=National Landscapes |language=en-GB}}</ref> previously the "National Association for Areas of Outstanding Natural Beauty" (NAAONB), an independent registered charity in England and Wales<ref>{{Cite web |title=NATIONAL LANDSCAPES ASSOCIATION - Charity 1158871 |url=https://register-of-charities.charitycommission.gov.uk/en/charity-search/-/charity-details/5050798/full-print |access-date=2026-02-23 |website=prd-ds-register-of-charities.charitycommission.gov.uk |language=en-GB}}</ref> acting on behalf of AONBs and their partners, which had used the slogan "Landscapes for Life".<ref name="aaonb">{{cite web |title=Landscapes for Life |url=https://landscapesforlife.org.uk/ |publisher=Association for AONBs |access-date=27 September 2019}}</ref>
43:AONBs in Northern Ireland are designated under separate legislation, originally under the Amenity Lands (NI) Act 1965; later replaced by the Nature Conservation and Amenity Lands (NI) Order 1985.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.doeni.gov.uk/niea/protected_areas_home/aonb.htm|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20140902035244/http://www.doeni.gov.uk/niea/protected_areas_home/aonb.htm|url-status=dead|title=Northern Ireland Environment Agency|archivedate=2 September 2014}}</ref><ref name=":19">{{Cite web |title=The Nature Conservation and Amenity Lands (Northern Ireland) Order 1985|url=https://www.legislation.gov.uk/nisi/1985/170/made|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230804100845/https://www.legislation.gov.uk/nisi/1985/170/made|archive-date=2023-08-04|access-date=2026-02-07|website=www.legislation.gov.uk|language=en}}</ref>'''<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |date=2015-09-21|title=When is NIEA consulted? {{!}} Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs|url=https://www.daera-ni.gov.uk/articles/when-niea-consulted|access-date=2026-02-07|website=www.daera-ni.gov.uk|language=en}}</ref>''' The [[Northern Ireland Environment Agency]] (part of the [[Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs]]<ref>{{Cite web |date=2015-08-26|title=Northern Ireland Environment Agency {{!}} Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs|url=https://www.daera-ni.gov.uk/articles/northern-ireland-environment-agency|access-date=2026-02-08|website=www.daera-ni.gov.uk|language=en}}</ref> of the [[Northern Ireland Executive]]) is responsible for designating AONBs in Northern Ireland, and facilitates their management.'''<ref name=":7">{{Cite web |date=June 2023|title=Mourne Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty Management Plan 2023 – 2027|url=https://cdn.ringofgullion.org/sites/2/2023/08/Mourne-AONB-Management-Plan-2023-27-June-2023.pdf|publisher=Mourne Heritage Trust}}</ref>'''

48:[[File:Amexstadjuly10.jpg|thumb|[[Falmer Stadium]] under construction in 2010 in the former [[Sussex Downs AONB]]]]
49:There are growing concerns among environmental and countryside groups that AONB status is increasingly under threat from development. The [[Campaign to Protect Rural England]] said in July 2006 that many AONBs were under greater threat than ever before.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.cpre.org.uk/news-releases/news-rel-2006/33-06.htm|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060926031151/http://www.cpre.org.uk/news-releases/news-rel-2006/33-06.htm|url-status=dead|archive-date=26 September 2006|title=CPRE : News releases : Outstandingly beautiful, still seriously threatened|date=26 September 2006|access-date=16 February 2018}}</ref> Three particular AONBs were cited: the [[Dorset AONB]] threatened by a road plan, the threat of a football stadium in the [[Sussex Downs AONB]], and, larger than any other, a £1 billion plan by [[Imperial College London]] to build thousands of houses and offices on hundreds of acres of AONB land on the [[Kent Downs]] at [[Wye, Kent|Wye]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.save-wye.org |title=save-wye.org |publisher=save-wye.org |access-date=30 June 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090507080241/http://www.save-wye.org/ |archive-date=7 May 2009 |url-status=dead }}</ref> The plan was eventually abandoned in 2006 after sustained local opposition. However, in September 2007 government approval was finally given for the development of a new football ground for [[Brighton and Hove Albion]] within the boundaries of the Sussex Downs AONB, after a fierce fight by conservationists. The subsequent development, known as [[Falmer Stadium]], was officially opened in July 2011. The Weymouth Relief Road in Dorset was constructed between 2008 and 2011, after environmental groups lost a High Court challenge to prevent its construction.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-england-dorset-12771624|title=Relief road opens after 60 years|work=BBC News |date=17 March 2011|access-date=16 February 2018}}</ref>
51:Writing in 2006, Professor Adrian Phillips listed threats facing AONBs, which he says include uncertainty over future support for land management, increasing development pressures, the impacts of globalization, and [[climate change]]. More subtle threats include creeping suburbanization and [[Glossary of equestrian terms#H|horsiculture]].<ref name="AONB story" />
54:[[Poet Laureate of the United Kingdom|Poet Laureate]] [[Simon Armitage]] wrote a poem "Fugitives", commissioned by the National Association of AONBs, which he read on [[Arnside Knott]] on 21 September 2019 to launch the celebration of the 70th anniversary of the [[National Parks and Access to the Countryside Act 1949|National Parks and Access to the Countryside Act]].<ref name="aonb-fugitives">{{cite web |title=Celebrating our special landscapes |url=https://www.arnsidesilverdaleaonb.org.uk/celebrating-special-landscapes/ |publisher=Arnside and Silverdale Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty |access-date=27 September 2019 |date=23 September 2019}}</ref><ref name="ecologist">{{cite news |title=Poem commissioned to celebrate national parks |url=https://theecologist.org/2019/sep/25/poem-commissioned-celebrate-national-parks |work=Ecologist |date=25 September 2019| access-date=27 September 2019}}</ref><ref name="fugitives">{{cite web |last1=Armitage |first1=Simon |title=Fugitives |url=https://www.simonarmitage.com/wp-content/uploads/Fugitives.pdf |access-date=27 September 2019}}</ref>

AONBs cover around 15% of England and 4% of Wales.<ref>{{Cite web |title=About Areas of Outstanding Natural Beauty (AONB's) |url=https://landscapesforlife.org.uk/about-aonbs/about-aonbs |access-date=2022-04-10 |website=landscapesforlife.org.uk}}</ref>
37:Areas of Outstanding Natural Beauty in [[England and Wales]] (now also National Landscapes) were originally created under the same legislation as the [[national park]]s, the [[National Parks and Access to the Countryside Act 1949]]. Unlike AONBs, national parks have special legal powers to prevent unsympathetic development. AONBs in general remain the responsibility of their local authorities by means of special committees that include members appointed by a [[Secretary of State (United Kingdom)|minister]] and by parishes, and only very limited statutory duties were imposed on local authorities within an AONB by the original 1949 Act. However, further regulation and protection of AONBs in England and Wales was added by the [[Countryside and Rights of Way Act 2000|Countryside and Rights of Way (CRoW) Act 2000]], under which new designations are now made,<ref>[http://www.staffsmoorlands.gov.uk/sites/default/files/documents/pages/CV%20AONB%20Assessment%20Paper.pdf Staffordshire Moorlands District Council] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140911183009/http://www.staffsmoorlands.gov.uk/sites/default/files/documents/pages/CV%20AONB%20Assessment%20Paper.pdf |date=11 September 2014 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.highweald.org/downloads/publications/1093-development-control-information-leaflet/file.html|title=High Weald AONB|access-date=16 February 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180928071108/http://www.highweald.org/downloads/publications/1093-development-control-information-leaflet/file.html|archive-date=28 September 2018|url-status=dead}}</ref>
39:In the [[National Planning Policy Framework]] (March 2012), the government stated that AONBs and national parks have equal status when it comes to planning decisions on landscape issues.  Two of the AONBs (the Cotswolds and the Chilterns), which extend into a large number of local authority areas, have their own statutory bodies, known as conservation boards. In 2019, the [[Julian Glover (journalist)|Glover Report]] made various recommendations regarding the future of AONBs{{snd}}the report's 'central proposal' being to bring [[National parks of the United Kingdom|National Parks]] and AONBs together as part of one 'family of national landscapes'.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Landscapes review: National Parks and AONBs |url=https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/designated-landscapes-national-parks-and-aonbs-2018-review |access-date=2022-06-03 |website=GOV.UK |date=25 September 2019 |language=en}}</ref> Following the report the Cotswolds Conservation Board announced in September 2020 that they were re-styling the area name and it is now known as the Cotswolds National Landscape.<ref>{{cite web |title=Latest News: The Cotswolds AONB gets a new look and a new name |url=https://www.cotswoldsaonb.org.uk/about-us/latest-news/ |website=Cotswolds National Landscape |publisher=Cotswolds AONB |access-date=31 October 2020}}</ref> The UK Government later accepted the report's recommendation for the AONBs in England to use "National Landscape".<ref>{{Cite web |title=Landscapes review (National Parks and AONBs): government response |url=https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/landscapes-review-national-parks-and-aonbs-government-response/landscapes-review-national-parks-and-aonbs-government-response |access-date=2026-02-23 |website=GOV.UK |language=en}}</ref>
41:All English and Welsh AONBs have a dedicated AONB officer and other staff. As required by the CRoW Act, each AONB has a management plan that sets out the characteristics and special qualities of the landscape and how they will be conserved and enhanced. The AONBs are collectively represented by the "National Landscapes Association",<ref>{{Cite web |title=National Landscapes - Our Story |url=https://national-landscapes.org.uk/about |access-date=2026-02-23 |website=National Landscapes |language=en-GB}}</ref> previously the "National Association for Areas of Outstanding Natural Beauty" (NAAONB), an independent registered charity in England and Wales<ref>{{Cite web |title=NATIONAL LANDSCAPES ASSOCIATION - Charity 1158871 |url=https://register-of-charities.charitycommission.gov.uk/en/charity-search/-/charity-details/5050798/full-print |access-date=2026-02-23 |website=prd-ds-register-of-charities.charitycommission.gov.uk |language=en-GB}}</ref> acting on behalf of AONBs and their partners, which had used the slogan "Landscapes for Life".<ref name="aaonb">{{cite web |title=Landscapes for Life |url=https://landscapesforlife.org.uk/ |publisher=Association for AONBs |access-date=27 September 2019}}</ref>
43:AONBs in Northern Ireland are designated under separate legislation, originally under the Amenity Lands (NI) Act 1965; later replaced by the Nature Conservation and Amenity Lands (NI) Order 1985.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.doeni.gov.uk/niea/protected_areas_home/aonb.htm|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20140902035244/http://www.doeni.gov.uk/niea/protected_areas_home/aonb.htm|url-status=dead|title=Northern Ireland Environment Agency|archivedate=2 September 2014}}</ref><ref name=":19">{{Cite web |title=The Nature Conservation and Amenity Lands (Northern Ireland) Order 1985|url=https://www.legislation.gov.uk/nisi/1985/170/made|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230804100845/https://www.legislation.gov.uk/nisi/1985/170/made|archive-date=2023-08-04|access-date=2026-02-07|website=www.legislation.gov.uk|language=en}}</ref>'''<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |date=2015-09-21|title=When is NIEA consulted? {{!}} Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs|url=https://www.daera-ni.gov.uk/articles/when-niea-consulted|access-date=2026-02-07|website=www.daera-ni.gov.uk|language=en}}</ref>''' The [[Northern Ireland Environment Agency]] (part of the [[Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs]]<ref>{{Cite web |date=2015-08-26|title=Northern Ireland Environment Agency {{!}} Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs|url=https://www.daera-ni.gov.uk/articles/northern-ireland-environment-agency|access-date=2026-02-08|website=www.daera-ni.gov.uk|language=en}}</ref> of the [[Northern Ireland Executive]]) is responsible for designating AONBs in Northern Ireland, and facilitates their management.'''<ref name=":7">{{Cite web |date=June 2023|title=Mourne Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty Management Plan 2023 – 2027|url=https://cdn.ringofgullion.org/sites/2/2023/08/Mourne-AONB-Management-Plan-2023-27-June-2023.pdf|publisher=Mourne Heritage Trust}}</ref>'''
45:On 22 November 2023, following a 2022 Landscapes Review policy paper by [[Julian Glover (journalist)|Julian Glover]],<ref>{{cite web |date=15 January 2022 |title=Landscapes review (National Parks and AONBs): government response |url=https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/landscapes-review-national-parks-and-aonbs-government-response/landscapes-review-national-parks-and-aonbs-government-response |accessdate=22 November 2023}}</ref> the AONBs in England and Wales adopted the National Landscapes name, and subsequently rebranded.<ref name="nlwelcome">{{cite web |date=22 November 2023 |title=Welcome to National Landscapes |url=https://national-landscapes.org.uk/news/welcome-to-national-landscapes |access-date=22 November 2023 |website=National Landscapes}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |date=22 November 2023 |title=National Landscapes: name change for AONBs represents ambitious plan to combat climate change and biodiversity loss in Britain |url=https://www.countryfile.com/news/aonbs-renamed-national-landscapes |accessdate=22 November 2023 |website=BBC Countryfile}}</ref> The name "area of outstanding natural beauty" is still the designated legal term.<ref>[https://cornwall-landscape.org/ Cornwall National Landscape], accessed 23 June 2024</ref> The review did not extend to Northern Ireland, and its AONBs did not adopt the new name.<ref>{{Cite web |title=National Landscapes |url=https://national-landscapes.org.uk/nations/northern-ireland |access-date=2025-05-05 |website=National Landscapes |language=en-GB}}</ref>
48:[[File:Amexstadjuly10.jpg|thumb|[[Falmer Stadium]] under construction in 2010 in the former [[Sussex Downs AONB]]]]
49:There are growing concerns among environmental and countryside groups that AONB status is increasingly under threat from development. The [[Campaign to Protect Rural England]] said in July 2006 that many AONBs were under greater threat than ever before.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.cpre.org.uk/news-releases/news-rel-2006/33-06.htm|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060926031151/http://www.cpre.org.uk/news-releases/news-rel-2006/33-06.htm|url-status=dead|archive-date=26 September 2006|title=CPRE : News releases : Outstandingly beautiful, still seriously threatened|date=26 September 2006|access-date=16 February 2018}}</ref> Three particular AONBs were cited: the [[Dorset AONB]] threatened by a road plan, the threat of a football stadium in the [[Sussex Downs AONB]], and, larger than any other, a £1 billion plan by [[Imperial College London]] to build thousands of houses and offices on hundreds of acres of AONB land on the [[Kent Downs]] at [[Wye, Kent|Wye]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.save-wye.org |title=save-wye.org |publisher=save-wye.org |access-date=30 June 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090507080241/http://www.save-wye.org/ |archive-date=7 May 2009 |url-status=dead }}</ref> The plan was eventually abandoned in 2006 after sustained local opposition. However, in September 2007 government approval was finally given for the development of a new football ground for [[Brighton and Hove Albion]] within the boundaries of the Sussex Downs AONB, after a fierce fight by conservationists. The subsequent development, known as [[Falmer Stadium]], was officially opened in July 2011. The Weymouth Relief Road in Dorset was constructed between 2008 and 2011, after environmental groups lost a High Court challenge to prevent its construction.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-england-dorset-12771624|title=Relief road opens after 60 years|work=BBC News |date=17 March 2011|access-date=16 February 2018}}</ref>
51:Writing in 2006, Professor Adrian Phillips listed threats facing AONBs, which he says include uncertainty over future support for land management, increasing development pressures, the impacts of globalization, and [[climate change]]. More subtle threats include creeping suburbanization and [[Glossary of equestrian terms#H|horsiculture]].<ref name="AONB story" />
54:[[Poet Laureate of the United Kingdom|Poet Laureate]] [[Simon Armitage]] wrote a poem "Fugitives", commissioned by the National Association of AONBs, which he read on [[Arnside Knott]] on 21 September 2019 to launch the celebration of the 70th anniversary of the [[National Parks and Access to the Countryside Act 1949|National Parks and Access to the Countryside Act]].<ref name="aonb-fugitives">{{cite web |title=Celebrating our special landscapes |url=https://www.arnsidesilverdaleaonb.org.uk/celebrating-special-landscapes/ |publisher=Arnside and Silverdale Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty |access-date=27 September 2019 |date=23 September 2019}}</ref><ref name="ecologist">{{cite news |title=Poem commissioned to celebrate national parks |url=https://theecologist.org/2019/sep/25/poem-commissioned-celebrate-national-parks |work=Ecologist |date=25 September 2019| access-date=27 September 2019}}</ref><ref name="fugitives">{{cite web |last1=Armitage |first1=Simon |title=Fugitives |url=https://www.simonarmitage.com/wp-content/uploads/Fugitives.pdf |access-date=27 September 2019}}</ref>

There are currently 40 national scenic areas (NSAs) in Scotland, covering 13% of the land area of Scotland.{{cite web|url=https://www.nature.scot/professional-advice/protected-areas-and-species/protected-areas/national-designations/national-scenic-areas/|title=National Scenic Areas|publisher=NatureScot|access-date=3 September 2020}} The areas protected by the designation are considered to represent the type of scenic beauty "popularly associated with Scotland and for which it is renowned".{{cite web|url=http://www.gov.scot/Topics/Environment/Countryside/Heritage/Areas|title=Countryside and Landscape in Scotland - National Scenic Areas|publisher=Scottish Government|date=2017-07-04|access-date=2018-01-31|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180131201226/http://www.gov.scot/Topics/Environment/Countryside/Heritage/Areas|archive-date=2018-01-31|url-status=dead}} As such they tend to be mainly found in remote and mountainous areas, with a review in 1997 noting a potential weakness of national scenic areas was that the original selection placed undue emphasis on [[Mountains and hills of Scotland|mountainous parts of the country]].{{cite web|url=http://www.snh.org.uk/pdfs/nsa/advicetogovernment.pdf|title=National Scenic Areas Review|publisher=Scottish Natural Heritage|date=1997|access-date=2018-02-05|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180206002610/http://www.snh.org.uk/pdfs/nsa/advicetogovernment.pdf|archive-date=2018-02-06|url-status=dead}} National scenic areas do however also cover seascapes, with approximately 26% of the total area protected by the designation being marine. The designation is primarily concerned with scenic qualities, although designated national scenic areas may well have other special qualities, for example related to culture, history, archaeology, geology or wildlife. Within the [[United Kingdom]] the NSA designation is regarded as equivalent to the [[Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty|Areas of Outstanding Natural Beauty]] (AONBs) of [[England]], [[Wales]] and [[Northern Ireland]]. The national scenic area designation does not have a high profile when compared to other [[protected areas of Scotland|conservation designations used in Scotland]]: in 2018 a survey by the [[National Trust for Scotland]] found that only 20% of Scots were "definitely aware" of national scenic areas, compared to 80% for National Parks.{{cite web|url=https://www.nts.org.uk/stories/scots-want-their-scenic-landscapes-better-protected|title=Scots want their scenic landscapes better protected|date=7 November 2018|publisher=National Trust for Scotland|access-date=28 April 2021}} ==History== [[File:main ridge of the cuillin in skye arp.jpg|thumb|The [[Cuillin|Cuillin Hills]] national scenic area.]] After the [[Second World War]], the [[Attlee ministry|Labour government]] passed the [[National Parks and Access to the Countryside Act 1949]], which led to the creation of ten [[national parks of England and Wales|national parks in England and Wales]] between 1951 and 1957, although no parks were created in Scotland. A committee, chaired by Sir Douglas Ramsay, was however established to consider preservation of the landscape in Scotland. The report, published in 1945, proposed that five areas (Loch Lomond & the Trossachs, the Cairngorms, Glen Coe-Ben Nevis-Black Mount, Wester Ross and Glen Strathfarrar-Glen Affric-Glen Cannich) should receive a level of protection.{{cite web|url=http://cairngormslearningzone.co.uk/managing-the-park/the-national-park-family/history-leading-to-the-cairngorms-national-park/|title=History Leading to the Cairngorms National Park|publisher=Cairngorms National Park Authority|access-date=2018-01-15|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180115185119/http://cairngormslearningzone.co.uk/managing-the-park/the-national-park-family/history-leading-to-the-cairngorms-national-park/|archive-date=2018-01-15|url-status=dead}} Accordingly, the government designated these areas as "national park direction areas", giving powers for planning decisions taken by local authorities to be reviewed by central government. After a further review of landscape protection in 1978, additional areas were identified for protection, and in 1981 the direction areas were replaced by national scenic areas, which were based on the 1978 recommendations. Following the passage of the [[National Parks (Scotland) Act 2000]], two [[national parks]] were established: [[Loch Lomond and The Trossachs National Park]] and the [[Cairngorms National Park]].{{cite web|url=https://www.nature.scot/professional-advice/protected-areas-and-species/protected-areas/national-designations/national-park |title=National Park|publisher=NatureScot|access-date=28 April 2021}} Both of these parks included areas that were already designated as national scenic areas, and the NSA designation remains in place alongside national park status for the areas in question. [[NatureScot|Scottish Natural Heritage]] reviewed the national scenic areas between November 2007 and March 2009 to try to identify what makes the scenery of each NSA special; however no formal review into the number and extent has been undertaken since the original report. In September 2017 the Scottish Parliament's Public Petitions Committee asked the government to explain why it is not reviewing the NSAs.{{cite web|url= https://archive2021.parliament.scot/parliamentarybusiness/report.aspx?r=11088&mode=pdf|title=Public Petitions Committee: Official Report|publisher=Scottish Parliament|date=14 September 2017|access-date=28 April 2021|pages=1–13}} ==Operation== [[File:Kyles-of-bute-2013-10-12.jpg|thumb|350px|The [[Kyles of Bute]] national scenic area in [[Argyll and Bute]].]] NSAs are currently designated under the [[Planning etc. (Scotland) Act 2006]]: all 40 current NSAs were redesignated under this act via a single order in 2010.
